summary: Studies throughput limits for single-packet messages on the ARPANET, motivated by sending digitized speech, which needs high throughput for small messages. It finds that throughput degrades for such messages.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending voice needs lots of tiny messages quickly. This paper checks how well the network handles them.

questions: why did single packet messages get slow on the arpanet
could you send voice over the arpanet
subtitle: Why sending many small messages through the ARPANET got stuck in a loop.

tldr.problem: Digitized speech and other applications need to send small messages rapidly, but the ARPANET's flow control mechanism caused single-packet messages to be retransmitted excessively when they arrived out of order.
tldr.mechanism: When a single-packet message arrives out of order, the destination IMP waits for the in-order message. A subsequent message arriving out of order can trigger a retransmission chain where all following messages are retransmitted repeatedly, reducing throughput to about one-fourth of expected.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes two solutions: either reject single-packet messages only when buffer requirements are unknown, or accept all single-packet messages and delete later those that cause buffer shortages, neither of which had been implemented yet.

today: RFC 632 identified a performance pathology in ARPANET flow control that later network designs worked to avoid. Modern networks use different mechanisms to balance ordering guarantees with throughput for small messages.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 632 examines throughput limitations for single-packet messages on the ARPANET, motivated by emerging interest in transmitting digitized speech over the network. Unlike interactive sessions or file transfers, speech transmission demands high throughput for small messages. A test on April 1, 1974 sending single-packet messages from MOFFET to SRI showed throughput of only 8 kilobits per second, about one-fourth of the expected 30+ kilobits, despite low channel utilization and no interfering traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests showed that sending voice over the network got stuck going very slow, even though the network had plenty of capacity.

sections.title: The Retransmission Problem
sections.content: When a single-packet message arrives out of order at the destination IMP, it is rejected and treated as a buffer allocation request. The message can only be retransmitted after the out-of-order acknowledgment (RFNM) is processed. If a single-packet message arrives before its predecessor, it triggers a chain where the out-of-order message and all subsequent messages remain unacknowledged until the earlier message can be delivered. In RFNM-driven traffic, this causes the entire stream to be retransmitted repeatedly, with round-trip times more than four times normal and the system trapped in this degraded state indefinitely unless the input stream is interrupted.
sections.plainLanguage: One message arriving out of order makes the system think all the following messages are also wrong, so it retransmits them over and over, clogging the network.

sections.title: Proposed Fixes
sections.content: The RFC proposes two solutions. The first rejects out-of-order single-packet messages only when the buffer requirements for earlier messages are unknown; once those buffers are allocated, out-of-order messages can be accepted without deadlock. The second solution accepts all single-packet messages initially, then deletes them if buffer space is needed, since source IMPs keep copies of unacknowledged messages. The RFC notes that a simple reservation of buffers for single-packet messages alone cannot fully solve this without deadlock risk, but either approach would avoid the sustained retransmission cycle that degrades speech transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ideas: either only block messages when you really don't know how much space you need, or accept everything and throw away copies when you run out of room.

references.text: Opderbeck, H., "Throughput Degradations for Single Packet Messages", RFC 632, May 1974.
